_meta.title: MediVision Copilot knowledge base
_meta.note: Original educational summaries written for this project. General references only (no copied text). Not medical advice.

entries.name: Atelectasis
entries.definition: Incomplete expansion or collapse of part of a lung, so that region holds less air than normal.
entries.appearance: Increased density with signs of volume loss: linear or wedge-shaped opacity, displacement of fissures, elevation of the hemidiaphragm or shift of the mediastinum toward the affected side.
causes: shallow breathing after surgery or with pain
airway obstruction (mucus plug, tumour, foreign body)
differential: consolidation (pneumonia) — usually no volume loss and may show air bronchograms
next_steps: Correlate with symptoms, oxygenation and recent surgery or immobility.
Follow-up radiograph after physiotherapy / deep breathing if clinically appropriate.
Persistent lobar collapse in an adult may warrant CT or bronchoscopy to exclude a central obstruction.
entries.urgency: Usually routine; lobar or whole-lung collapse can be urgent.
entries.lay: A part of the lung is not fully inflated, a bit like a balloon that is partly deflated. It is common after surgery or when breathing is shallow, and often improves with deep breathing exercises.
references: Fleischner Society: Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging (Hansell et al., Radiology 2008)

entries.name: Cardiomegaly
entries.definition: Enlargement of the cardiac silhouette on a chest radiograph, classically a cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) above 0.5 on a PA view.
entries.appearance: Widened heart shadow relative to the chest width. AP and supine films magnify the heart, so CTR > 0.5 on those views is less reliable.
next_steps: Check the projection (PA vs AP) and degree of inspiration before concluding.
Clinical correlation; echocardiography is the usual next test to assess cardiac size and function.
Compare with prior imaging for change.
entries.urgency: Usually routine unless new and associated with pulmonary oedema.
entries.lay: The heart looks larger than usual on the X-ray. This can have many causes, and an ultrasound of the heart (echocardiogram) is often used to check how it is working.
references: Danzer CS. The cardiothoracic ratio. Am J Med Sci 1919
Fleischner Society glossary (2008)

entries.name: Pleural effusion
entries.definition: An abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall.
entries.appearance: Blunting of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus-shaped opacity at the lung base; large effusions opacify the hemithorax and may push the mediastinum away.
next_steps: Clinical correlation; ultrasound confirms fluid and guides sampling.
Large or unexplained effusions may need thoracentesis (pleural fluid analysis).
Follow-up imaging to confirm resolution.
entries.urgency: Moderate; large or rapidly enlarging effusions causing breathlessness are urgent.
entries.lay: There is some fluid collected around the lung. Doctors look for the cause, and sometimes drain a sample with a needle to test it.
references: BTS guideline for pleural disease (Roberts et al., Thorax 2023)

entries.name: Infiltration
entries.definition: A non-specific term (used as a label in the NIH dataset) for an area of increased lung density that is not normally there.
entries.appearance: Ill-defined hazy or patchy opacity. Radiologists now prefer more specific descriptions (consolidation, ground-glass, reticular).
next_steps: Describe the pattern and distribution; correlate clinically.
Short-interval follow-up if infection is suspected, to confirm resolution.
entries.urgency: Depends on cause; usually routine to moderate.
entries.lay: Part of the lung looks hazier than usual. This is a general description, and doctors combine it with symptoms to work out the cause.
references: Fleischner Society glossary (2008) — recommends against the term 'infiltrate'

entries.name: Mass
entries.definition: A rounded opacity in the lung larger than 3 cm in diameter.
entries.appearance: Well- or ill-defined round or lobulated opacity; may show cavitation, spiculation or associated lymph node enlargement.
next_steps: CT chest with contrast is usually recommended to characterise a new mass.
Compare with prior imaging; discuss with the respiratory / thoracic oncology team.
Tissue sampling may be needed depending on CT features.
entries.urgency: High — a new mass needs prompt work-up.
entries.lay: There is a larger spot on the lung picture. It needs further tests, usually a CT scan, to find out what it is.
references: Fleischner Society glossary (2008)
BTS guidelines for pulmonary nodules (Callister et al., Thorax 2015)

entries.name: Nodule
entries.definition: A rounded opacity up to 3 cm in diameter, surrounded by lung.
entries.appearance: Small round density; many are better seen on CT. Calcification patterns can suggest a benign cause.
next_steps: Management of incidental nodules follows size- and risk-based guidance (e.g. the Fleischner Society 2017 guidelines for CT-detected nodules).
Compare with prior imaging for stability; CT may be recommended to characterise.
entries.urgency: Usually routine follow-up; larger or growing nodules are more urgent.
entries.lay: There is a small spot on the lung. Most such spots are harmless, but doctors may suggest a follow-up scan to make sure it does not change.
references: MacMahon H. et al. Guidelines for management of incidental pulmonary nodules detected on CT images: Fleischner Society 2017. Radiology 2017

entries.name: Pneumonia
entries.definition: Infection of the lung tissue; on imaging it usually appears as consolidation.
entries.appearance: Patchy or lobar consolidation, sometimes with air bronchograms; may be accompanied by a small effusion.
next_steps: Diagnosis is clinical + radiological: correlate with fever, cough, oxygen levels and blood tests.
Follow-up radiograph after treatment (often ~6 weeks in older adults) to confirm resolution.
entries.urgency: Moderate to high, especially with low oxygen levels.
entries.lay: The X-ray shows changes that can be caused by a lung infection. Doctors combine this with symptoms and tests to decide on treatment, such as antibiotics.
references: NICE guideline NG138/CG191 (pneumonia in adults)

entries.name: Pneumothorax
entries.definition: Air in the pleural space, separating the lung from the chest wall and causing partial or complete lung collapse.
entries.appearance: A thin visceral pleural line with absent lung markings beyond it, typically at the apex on an upright film. Tension pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum away.
next_steps: Urgent clinical assessment; tension physiology is an emergency.
Management (observation, aspiration, chest drain) depends on size and symptoms.
Repeat imaging to confirm re-expansion.
entries.urgency: High — potentially life-threatening; flag for immediate review.
entries.lay: Air has leaked into the space around the lung, which can make the lung partly collapse. This needs to be checked by a doctor promptly.
references: BTS guideline for pleural disease (Roberts et al., Thorax 2023)

entries.name: Consolidation
entries.definition: Replacement of air in the alveoli by fluid, pus, blood or cells, making that part of the lung appear solid (white) on X-ray.
entries.appearance: Homogeneous opacity that obscures vessels, often with air bronchograms and without volume loss.
next_steps: Clinical correlation for infection.
Follow-up imaging to document resolution, especially in smokers and older adults.
entries.urgency: Moderate to high depending on extent and clinical state.
entries.lay: Part of the lung looks solid instead of airy, often because of infection or fluid. Doctors check symptoms and tests to find the cause.
references: Fleischner Society glossary (2008)

entries.name: Pulmonary oedema
entries.definition: Excess fluid in the lung interstitium and/or alveoli.
entries.appearance: Upper-lobe blood diversion, Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing, bilateral perihilar ('bat-wing') opacity, often with effusions and cardiomegaly in cardiac causes.
next_steps: Urgent clinical correlation (breathlessness, oxygen, fluid balance).
Cardiac assessment (BNP, echocardiography) if cardiogenic cause suspected.
Follow-up radiograph to monitor response.
entries.lay: There is extra fluid in the lungs, often related to how the heart is pumping. Doctors usually treat this promptly.
references: ESC heart failure guidelines (McDonagh et al., Eur Heart J 2021)

entries.name: Emphysema
entries.definition: Permanent enlargement of airspaces beyond the terminal bronchioles with destruction of their walls; part of COPD.
entries.appearance: Hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragms, increased retrosternal air space, reduced vascular markings, bullae.
next_steps: Correlate with spirometry and smoking history.
CT better characterises extent if needed.
entries.lay: The lungs look over-inflated, a pattern often seen with long-term lung damage such as from smoking. Breathing tests help assess it.
references: GOLD 2024 report

entries.name: Fibrosis
entries.definition: Scarring of lung tissue that makes the lungs stiff.
entries.appearance: Reticular (net-like) opacities, often basal and peripheral, with volume loss; honeycombing in advanced disease (best seen on CT).
next_steps: High-resolution CT is the usual next test.
Respiratory referral and lung function tests if new.
entries.lay: There are signs of scarring in the lungs. A detailed CT scan and breathing tests help understand the cause and extent.
references: ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT IPF guideline (Raghu et al., AJRCCM 2022)

entries.name: Pleural thickening
entries.definition: Thickening of the pleural lining, often from old inflammation, infection or asbestos exposure.
entries.appearance: Smooth or irregular soft-tissue density along the chest wall or apex; plaques may calcify.
next_steps: Compare with prior imaging; stable thickening is usually benign.
CT if nodular, progressive or with occupational exposure.
entries.lay: The lining around the lung looks thicker, usually from old inflammation. It is often stable and harmless, but changes are checked.
references: Fleischner Society glossary (2008)

entries.name: Hiatus hernia
entries.definition: Part of the stomach (or other abdominal content) passing up through the diaphragm into the chest.
entries.appearance: Retrocardiac soft-tissue density, often with an air-fluid level behind the heart.
causes: age-related widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus
next_steps: Usually incidental; correlate with reflux symptoms.
Contrast study or endoscopy if symptomatic.
entries.lay: Part of the stomach sits slightly up into the chest through the muscle that separates them. This is common and often causes no problems.
references: General radiology texts

entries.name: Fracture
entries.definition: A break in the continuity of a bone.
entries.appearance: Lucent line through the bone, cortical step or buckle, displacement or angulation of fragments; some fractures are subtle and need extra views.
next_steps: Clinical examination for point tenderness; additional projections if suspicion remains.
Orthopaedic assessment for displaced or intra-articular fractures.
CT or MRI for occult fractures (e.g. scaphoid, hip) when clinically suspected.
entries.urgency: Moderate to high (displaced, open or hip fractures are urgent).
entries.lay: There may be a break in the bone. A doctor will examine the area and decide whether it needs a cast, splint or other treatment.
references: FracAtlas dataset paper (Abedeen et al., Sci Data 2023) for dataset context

entries.name: Glioma
entries.definition: A tumour arising from the glial (supporting) cells of the brain; grades range from slow-growing to aggressive.
entries.appearance: Intra-axial mass, often bright on FLAIR/T2; higher-grade tumours may enhance with contrast and show surrounding oedema or necrosis.
next_steps: Contrast-enhanced MRI with dedicated sequences.
Neurosurgical / neuro-oncology multidisciplinary review.
Tissue diagnosis guides treatment.
entries.lay: The scan shows a possible growth arising from the brain's supporting cells. Specialists will arrange further scans and discuss next steps.
references: WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed. (2021)

entries.name: Meningioma
entries.definition: A usually benign, slow-growing tumour arising from the meninges (the membranes covering the brain).
entries.appearance: Extra-axial, well-circumscribed mass with a broad dural base, often enhancing strongly ('dural tail').
causes: mostly unknown; more common in women and with age
next_steps: Contrast MRI to characterise.
Small asymptomatic meningiomas are often monitored with interval MRI; symptomatic ones are referred to neurosurgery.
entries.urgency: Usually moderate; depends on size and mass effect.
entries.lay: The scan shows a possible growth on the lining of the brain. These are usually slow-growing and often not cancer; doctors decide whether to monitor or treat.
references: EANO guideline on meningiomas (Goldbrunner et al., Lancet Oncol 2016/2021)

entries.name: Pituitary tumour
entries.definition: A growth in the pituitary gland at the base of the brain; most are benign adenomas.
entries.appearance: Sellar/suprasellar mass; larger ones may compress the optic chiasm.
next_steps: Dedicated pituitary MRI.
Endocrine blood tests and visual field assessment.
Endocrinology / neurosurgery referral.
entries.urgency: Moderate; urgent if visual loss or sudden headache (apoplexy).
entries.lay: There may be a growth on the pituitary gland, a small gland that controls hormones. These are usually not cancer; blood tests and a dedicated scan help plan care.
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidelines (pituitary incidentaloma, 2011)

entries.name: No tumour
entries.definition: The brain classifier's 'no tumour' class: no features of the three tumour types it was trained on.
entries.appearance: No mass lesion detected by the model on this slice.
differential: non-tumour pathology the model was not trained for (stroke, haemorrhage, MS)
next_steps: A single 2-D slice cannot exclude disease elsewhere; review the full study.
entries.lay: The model did not see signs of the tumour types it knows on this image. A specialist still reviews the full scan.

entries.name: Cardiothoracic ratio (CTR)
entries.definition: Maximal horizontal heart width divided by maximal internal thoracic width on a frontal chest X-ray. Above 0.5 on a PA film suggests cardiomegaly.
entries.appearance: MediVision estimates it from our lung-segmentation masks: thoracic width = widest outer lung-to-lung span; heart width = widest gap between the medial lung borders in the lower half.
next_steps: Treat the automatic CTR as an estimate; confirm visually.
entries.lay: A simple ratio comparing the width of the heart with the width of the chest.
references: Danzer CS 1919

entries.name: Grad-CAM heatmap
entries.definition: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping: highlights image regions that most increased the model's score for a chosen finding (Selvaraju et al., ICCV 2017). Grad-CAM++ refines it for multiple or small regions.
entries.appearance: Warm colours = regions that influenced the prediction most. It shows where the model looked, not proof of disease.
next_steps: If the heatmap highlights text markers, edges or devices, treat the prediction with suspicion (shortcut learning).
entries.lay: A colour map showing which parts of the image the AI paid most attention to.
references: Selvaraju R.R. et al. ICCV 2017
Chattopadhay A. et al. WACV 2018 (Grad-CAM++)

entries.name: Occlusion sensitivity
entries.definition: Model-agnostic explanation: patches of the image are blanked one at a time and the drop in the finding's probability is mapped.
entries.appearance: Bright regions = blanking them reduced the prediction most.
entries.lay: We hide small parts of the image and see which hidden parts change the AI's answer most.
references: Zeiler M.D., Fergus R. ECCV 2014

entries.name: Model uncertainty
entries.definition: MediVision combines two signals: disagreement between the three ensemble members (standard deviation) and Monte-Carlo dropout variance (the head is sampled several times with dropout on). Their combination is shown as the uncertainty whisker.
entries.appearance: High uncertainty means the models are not consistent — a cue for careful human review.
next_steps: Treat high-uncertainty findings as unreliable; review the image directly.
entries.lay: How much the AI's different 'opinions' disagree with each other.
references: Lakshminarayanan B. et al. NeurIPS 2017 (deep ensembles)
Gal Y., Ghahramani Z. ICML 2016 (MC dropout)

entries.name: Calibration (temperature scaling)
entries.definition: Adjusting model scores so that a predicted 30% means roughly 30% of such cases are positive. We fit one temperature per label and per model on the validation set (Guo et al., ICML 2017).
entries.appearance: The Lab page shows reliability diagrams before and after calibration (ECE).
entries.lay: Making the AI's percentages honest, so 70% really means 'about 7 in 10'.
references: Guo C. et al. ICML 2017

entries.name: Out-of-distribution (OOD) guard
entries.definition: Two safety checks: our modality router classifies each upload (chest X-ray / bone X-ray / brain MRI / other medical / not medical), and an energy score on the chest ensemble flags images unlike its training data.
entries.appearance: A warning banner appears for doubtful inputs; non-medical images are not analysed.
next_steps: Verify the image type and quality before trusting results.
entries.lay: A check that stops the AI from confidently analysing pictures it was never trained on.
references: Liu W. et al. NeurIPS 2020 (energy-based OOD)
Wang H. et al. NeurIPS 2021 (JointEnergy for multi-label)

entries.name: Triage / urgency score
entries.definition: A 0–100 score combining each positive finding's severity weight, how far its calibrated probability exceeds the operating threshold, and model confidence. Levels: CRITICAL ≥ 75, URGENT ≥ 45, ROUTINE (any positive or doubtful input), NORMAL.
entries.appearance: Shown as a coloured pill on the worklist; the weights are listed in the model card.
entries.lay: A priority score that helps decide which scans a doctor should look at first.

entries.name: Fleischner Society
entries.definition: An international society of thoracic radiology that publishes widely used guidance, e.g. a glossary of thoracic imaging terms (2008) and recommendations for managing incidental lung nodules seen on CT (2017).
entries.lay: An expert group whose recommendations doctors use for lung findings.
references: Hansell D.M. et al. Radiology 2008
MacMahon H. et al. Radiology 2017

entries.name: Federated learning
entries.definition: Training one model across several hospitals without moving patient images: each site trains locally and only model weights are averaged (FedAvg, McMahan et al. 2017).
entries.lay: Hospitals improve a shared AI together while each keeps its patients' images at home.
references: McMahan B. et al. AISTATS 2017

entries.name: Opacity
entries.definition: Any area that appears whiter (more attenuating) than expected on an X-ray. It is a descriptive term, not a diagnosis.
entries.appearance: Can be focal or diffuse, well or poorly defined.
next_steps: Characterise pattern and correlate clinically.
entries.lay: A whiter area on the X-ray that doctors look at more closely.
references: Fleischner Society glossary (2008)

entries.name: PA and AP views
entries.definition: PA (posterior-anterior) chest films are taken standing with the beam from back to front; AP films (front to back, often portable or supine) magnify the heart and can mimic cardiomegaly.
entries.lay: The direction the X-ray was taken from, which can change how big the heart looks.
